q: Which of the following was a key provision of Attlee's February 1947 statement regarding the transfer of power?
o: Power would be transferred only to a single unified central government under all circumstances
The British would retain control over defence indefinitely after transfer of power
Power might be transferred either to a central government or, in some areas, to existing provincial governments if the constituent assembly was not fully representative
All princely states would automatically become part of British India's successor government

q: According to Attlee's statement, what would happen to British paramountcy over the princely states upon transfer of power?
o: Paramountcy would be transferred exclusively to the Congress-led government
British powers and obligations toward the princely states would lapse, but would not automatically transfer to any successor government in British India
Paramountcy would be automatically transferred wholesale to whichever government succeeded British India
The princely states would remain permanently under British control even after independence

q: Why did the British government fix a specific date for withdrawal in the February 1947 statement?
o: Because international law required a fixed exit date for all colonial powers
Because the United Nations had imposed the deadline on Britain
To shock the parties into agreement, avert the deepening constitutional crisis, and convince Indians of British sincerity, given the irreversible decline in governmental authority
Because Indian industrialists demanded a fixed date for economic planning purposes

q: Why was the provision allowing transfer of power to more than one centre acceptable to the Congress?
o: It ensured the immediate abolition of the Muslim League as a political entity
It required unanimous approval from all princely states before proceeding
It guaranteed the Congress control over the entire subcontinent without any partition
It meant the existing constituent assembly could proceed to frame a constitution for the areas it represented, offering a way out of the deadlock

q: In April 1947, what message did Congress president Kripalani reportedly convey to the Viceroy regarding Pakistan?
o: That the Congress wanted a plebiscite held in every province of British India
That the Congress would never under any circumstances accept the idea of Pakistan
That the Congress demanded immediate merger of the Muslim League into itself
That the Congress would let the League have Pakistan, provided Bengal and Punjab were partitioned in a fair manner rather than fighting a battle over the issue

q: Why was Mountbatten able to act more firmly and quickly as Viceroy than his predecessors?
o: He was personally appointed by the Muslim League rather than the British Cabinet
He alone among Viceroys had prior administrative experience in India
He had significantly less oversight from the British Parliament than any previous Viceroy
He was informally given greater powers to decide matters on the spot and had the backing of Britain's firm decision to quit at the earliest

q: What was the 'Plan Balkan' that Mountbatten formulated between March and May 1947, before it was abandoned?
o: A plan to divide India into exactly two dominions with no options for individual provinces or states
A plan to transfer power to separate provinces or a confederation, with princely states free to join India, Pakistan, or remain independent
A plan to grant complete independence only to Bengal and Punjab while retaining British control elsewhere
A plan proposing continued British rule over a confederated India for another decade

q: Under the Mountbatten Plan of June 3, 1947, how were Punjab and Bengal's legislative assemblies to decide on partition?
o: Only the Muslim League members had voting rights on the question
They would meet in two groups (Hindu and Muslim members) to vote, with a simple majority in either group sufficing to trigger partition of that province
Decision was to be made solely by the Viceroy without any legislative vote
A single joint vote of the entire assembly, with a two-thirds majority required

q:
Which of the following outcomes did the Mountbatten Plan rule out, given the Congress's acceptance of a unified (if partitioned) India?
1. Independence for the princely states.
2. Independence for Bengal as a separate unit.
3. Accession of Hyderabad to Pakistan.
4. Setting up a Boundary Commission if partition occurred.
Which of these were ruled OUT (i.e., NOT permitted), rather than provided for?
o: Only 1
Only 4
1, 2 and 3 only

q: Who chaired the Boundary Commissions constituted to demarcate the borders of Punjab and Bengal after partition?
o: V.P. Menon
Lord Wavell
Sir Cyril Radcliffe
Lord Mountbatten

q: Why did Mountbatten decide to delay the public announcement of the Radcliffe Award, even though it was ready by August 12, 1947?
o: Because the princely states needed additional time to review the boundaries
Because Radcliffe himself requested additional time to revise his boundary lines
So that the British could escape responsibility for the resulting communal disturbances by having it announced only after the transfer of power on August 15
Because the Congress and League had not yet agreed to accept the award's contents

q: Following the referendum process, which of the following outcomes is correctly matched?
o: Both NWFP and Sylhet opted to remain outside both dominions
Both NWFP and Sylhet voted to join India
NWFP voted to join India, while Sylhet voted to remain independent
NWFP voted in favour of Pakistan (with the Provincial Congress abstaining from the referendum), while Sylhet's referendum resulted in its incorporation into East Bengal (Pakistan)

q: In the first phase of state integration, why did most princes agree relatively easily to sign the Instrument of Accession covering defence, external affairs and communication?
o: Because the Indian government offered them full sovereignty in exchange
Because the British government directly compelled them to sign under threat of force
Because they were merely 'surrendering' functions they never actually held (these had been part of British paramountcy), and their internal political structure remained unchanged
Because the accession was purely symbolic and carried no legal effect

q: What was the principal incentive ('bait') offered to princes during the more difficult second phase of state integration?
o: Exemption from all future taxation
A generous privy purse, along with appointments as governors and rajpramukhs in free India
Guaranteed seats in the Indian Parliament for life
Permanent retention of full sovereign powers over their territories

q: According to the chapter, which of the following best explains the deeper reason why the Congress ultimately accepted partition?
o: The Congress accepted partition purely due to Gandhi's personal insistence, against the wishes of all other leaders
Partition was solely the result of British military coercion against Congress wishes
The Congress fully supported partition from the very beginning of the freedom struggle as an ideological goal
The Congress had succeeded in building national consciousness to pressure Britain to leave, but had failed in its parallel task of fully integrating Muslims into a unified national identity

q: According to the chapter, in what way did Nehru display 'wishful thinking' regarding partition, underestimating the nature of 1940s communalism?
o: He believed communalism in the 1940s was identical in nature to that of the 1920s
He insisted from the outset that partition was permanent and irreversible
He believed Hindu-Muslim differences would be patched up once the British left, that partition was only temporary, and that it would be peaceful once Pakistan was conceded
He predicted correctly and accurately that partition would cause massive, prolonged violence

q: Why did Gandhi feel a sense of helplessness regarding the acceptance of partition?
o: He believed the people themselves had become communalised, making it impossible to sustain a movement against communalism, though he urged Congressmen not to accept partition 'in their hearts'
He believed partition was entirely his own idea and felt guilty for proposing it
He had no opinion on partition and remained indifferent throughout the process
He believed partition was the best possible outcome and celebrated its acceptance

q: According to historian R.C. Mazumdar's assessment (as cited in the chapter), what combination of factors is credited with bringing freedom to India, beyond the Civil Disobedience Movement alone?
o: The cumulative effect of Gandhi's campaigns, the INA's efforts under Bose, and the indirect pressure exerted by Hitler and Japan against Britain during the two World Wars
Only the direct diplomatic intervention of the United States and Soviet Union
Exclusively the Civil Disobedience Movement, with no role for any other factor
Solely the economic collapse of British India with no political factors involved

q: According to the chapter, which factor made it clear to the exhausted British that they could no longer rely on the loyalty of Indian soldiers for maintaining authority?
o: The revelations made during the INA trials and the popular reaction they produced across India
The failure of the Cripps Mission in 1942
The passage of the Government of India Act, 1935
The outcome of the 1937 provincial elections
